=== FILE: videos/2018-03-01_p43NDXHxQAQ_sleep-science-hacking-your-biological-clock-to-win/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: p43NDXHxQAQ
title: "SSAC18: Sleep Science Hacking your Biological Clock to Win"
event: SSAC18 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Nita Singh (caption spelling)]
topics: [sports-science, american-football, basketball, other-sport:baseball]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A sleep physician from the Henry Ford sleep disorder center argues that circadian timing is an under-used performance lever. She explains how the body clock sets alertness, when performance peaks, and why a chronotype (morning or night person) shifts that peak. She then covers jet lag in travelling teams and the two tools that move the clock, light and melatonin, with timing that matters. Three case examples follow (an NFL team going to London, an East Coast baseball team going west, a West Coast NBA team going east). The point is that travel plans should be built around body-clock time, not local time.

## Key claims

- More than half of genes and gene functions are driven by the biological clock [02:02].
- The master clock in the brain is set by light, which suppresses melatonin; at night melatonin is released and dampens the alerting signal [02:34].
- Two independent processes set sleepiness: a sleep drive that builds with time awake, and a clock-driven alerting signal; the afternoon dip is the clock, not the audience [04:09].
- Alerting signal and body temperature are lowest between 3:00 and 6:00 in the morning, which matters when shifting the clock [05:11].
- Coordination, reaction time, cardiovascular efficiency and strength peak in the evening, about 4:00 to 7:00 [06:11].
- Over 40 years of NFL night games, West Coast teams in 9:00 night games beat the point spread and won twice as often as the opposing side [07:12]; the speaker says this was replicated in the NBA and that more time zones crossed in baseball lowers win chance [07:42].
- A 20-year MLB study found East Coast teams returning from the West Coast lose the first home game because they are jet-lagged [07:42].
- Chronotype is inherited; in a study of competitive athletes the group peaked between 4 and 7 p.m., but night owls peaked later and morning types earlier [09:47], [10:19].
- Jet lag arises from crossing three or more time zones quickly and affects sleep, alertness, concentration, motivation and stomach [10:49].
- Light and melatonin are the two effective clock shifters: morning light advances the clock, night light delays it, and melatonin acts in the opposite direction to light [12:21], [13:21].
- Brighter light and blue-green wavelengths shift the clock more [13:51].
- Timing relative to body temperature minimum decides direction of shift; wrong-timed light makes things worse [14:21], [14:52].
- For the Saints London trip, players avoided light with UV-blocking sunglasses until about noon London time for three days, took supervised melatonin, banked sleep beforehand and switched to London time on the plane [16:23], [17:25], [18:28].
- Acclimatization normally takes about one day per time zone, and targeted steps can shift in a day [19:00].
- For the baseball team the aim was aligning peak performance to game time, using education, pre-shifting, light boxes and caffeine [20:31], [21:34].
- For the NBA team the advice was to not shift: stay on West Coast time, no morning practices, and stay overnight after the game instead of a red-eye [22:05], [22:36].
- Jet lag and sleep loss may leave athletes more open to the common cold, because immune cells have a rhythm and sleep loss lowers immunity [23:06].

## Numbers and definitions

- More than 50% of genes driven by the clock [02:02].
- Alerting signal and temperature minimum between 3:00 and 6:00 a.m. [05:11].
- Performance peak 4:00 to 7:00 p.m. [06:11].
- NFL: 40 years of data, West Coast teams win twice as often against the spread in night games [07:12].
- MLB: 20 years of data [07:42].
- Jet lag: three or more time zones [10:49].
- Light: 10,000 lux versus 1,500 lux, brighter is better [13:51].
- Saints game time about 2:30 p.m. London time; suggested bedtime about 11 p.m. and wake about 7:00 a.m. [14:52], [15:23]; sunglasses until about noon for the first three days [16:23].
- About one day per time zone to acclimatize [19:00].
- Caption garbles: "2:30" and the Saints sleep-time mapping (4:00 to 5:00 p.m. New Orleans time) are as captioned [15:53]; "red-eye" and "4:00 in the morning" for NBA are as captioned [22:36]. Chronotype study sample size not given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Two-process model of sleep (sleep drive and circadian alerting signal) [04:09].
- Light and melatonin timing relative to the temperature minimum [14:21].
- Chronotype assessment, shown by audience hand-raise on bedtime [08:43].
- Team travel protocols: pre-flight sleep banking, setting watches to destination time, plane sleep rules, sunglasses, strict bedtime, cold dark room [17:25], [19:00].

## Limits and open questions

- Case studies have no outcome data beyond reported better sleep and feeling refreshed for the Saints [19:30]; wins are mentioned but not attributed to the program.
- The speaker says light and melatonin are 100% effective in a sleep lab but travel adds many uncontrolled variables [16:54].
- The 40-year NFL and 20-year MLB findings are stated without sample sizes or effect estimates beyond "twice as often".
- Baseball and NBA teams are unnamed; interventions differ and are not compared.
- Presenter is a clinician describing her own practice, a professional view.
- Caption errors likely (for example "ear" for eye [02:34]).

## Summary

Two executives from Edge Sports and Edge Analytics present their football analytics product, built around game-winning chance (GWC) as the single objective for decisions. They use Super Bowl examples to show how a simulation engine scores fourth-down and punt calls, then describe season reports, a player evaluation model and a roster valuation tool for talent decisions. It is a vendor presentation, so the claims are the company's own and no validation data are shown. It matters as an example of a decision framework tied to one measurable objective.

## Key claims

- The framework: define the data available, how it turns into information, the constraints (the rules) and a clearly defined objective, here maximizing GWC [05:14], [05:45].
- The product simulates a game from kickoff or any set point using 20 years of play-by-play, then customizes each team from in-season data [02:37], [06:18].
- For the Super Bowl they customized both teams from 18 games of in-season data and had Philadelphia as a slight favorite at kickoff [06:50].
- Early second quarter: New England kicked a field goal on a short yardage situation; the simulation said going for it would win about 4% more often on average [08:21].
- With just under six minutes left, New England, trailing by a point, went for it at its own 45 rather than punting; the speakers put the impact at about 13 percent of GWC [09:23], [09:55].
- They say punting and pinning at the one-yard line would still have cost about 6% GWC [12:05].
- They argue the Eagles' confidence in going for it reflects a behavior shift in the NFL, including more third-down aggression [10:25].
- A season-end report compares assets and liabilities (decisions, execution, randomness) like an income statement; for New England it implied about 11 expected wins against 13 actual [13:37], [14:09].
- A player evaluation model, to be available that fall, cross-references scouting, performance, physiology and cognition data with team-set weights [15:09], [16:12].
- An Edge Power Index splits teams into special teams, offense and defensive pass, offense and defensive rush; a roster valuation tool is in development to relate roster changes to expected wins and spend [16:45], [17:16].

## Numbers and definitions

- GWC: game-winning chance, the objective (win probability) [05:45].
- Super Bowl customization: 18 games of in-season data [06:50].
- Field goal versus go on short yardage: about 4% more wins on average by going for it [08:21].
- Fourth-down punt versus go: about 13 percent impact [09:55]; punt pinning at the one-yard line: about 6% GWC lost [12:05].
- New England: about 11 predicted wins versus 13 actual (13-3) [14:09]; the captions at [13:37] say "13 regular season games."
- About seven billion simulations and pieces of analysis in a season [16:12]; captioned in the video trailer as "billions of customized simulations" [02:37]; "hundreds of thousands" of simulations per decision in Q&A [19:18].
- Caption problems: "Lisa doll" for Lee Sedol-type reference is as captioned [05:14]; "Philadelphia ... maybe had a couple more" chips is an analogy, not a number [07:50]. The 13% figure's exact baseline (percentage points of win probability) is not stated.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Simulation engine over play-by-play distributions with coach behavior, clock and timeouts [06:18].
- Team customization from in-season data, with user sensitivity testing (for example assume best rushing offense versus weakest rush defense) [19:48].
- Modules named: play call simulator, strategy guides, game day matchups, postgame and season reports, player evaluation, roster valuation, custom analytics [03:07], [03:39].
- Deep Blue and Go as the "game of skill" analogy for the approach [04:43], [05:14].

## Limits and open questions

- Product pitch; no validation, calibration or error rates are shown, and examples are two plays.
- The same decision is shown to depend on situation, yet the 4% figure is averaged over simulated outcomes [08:21], [19:48].
- The 11 versus 13 wins gap is attributed to several causes without showing the breakdown [14:09].
- Player evaluation does not model non-physical attributes itself; it only cross-references what the team gathers [21:20].
- The speakers say the model is customizable by coaches and that the staff knows its team better [20:49].

## Q&A

- Does the model account for variance, such as a favorite preferring a lower-variance play? The speaker says users can test sensitivities and extreme scenarios; they say it may change the size of the gap but does not necessarily flip it [18:16], [19:18], [20:19].
- How are non-physical player attributes quantified? It does not; it cross-references the objective data teams already collect and lets users weight it [21:20].

## Summary

A research-paper-competition talk that relates inertial sensor training load to non-contact time-loss injuries in football. It starts with the limits of earlier load and injury papers (binary injury coding, no censoring, small samples, thresholds that vary by team, retrospective rather than predictive) and cites work finding single-club models predict poorly on unseen data. The study followed 101 players for one season with 29 non-contact injuries. The best model combined total player load, low player load and high impacts: higher volume and higher physical intensity went with higher risk, and the speaker frames this as risk context for practitioners, not prediction.

## Key claims

- Non-contact injuries matter because they are thought to be partly due to training errors: too much too soon, too much for too long, or too little [03:03].
- Earlier papers often merge contact and non-contact injuries, mix time loss and non-time loss, skip censoring, give thresholds that differ across papers, and are retrospective [03:33], [04:04], [05:06], [06:08].
- A cited Australian football study found single-club injury models predicted poorly on unseen data [06:39], [07:10].
- The aim was to find associations between training load variables and non-contact time-loss injury, not to predict before a session [07:41].
- Metrics used were total player load, four player load effort bands, impacts (three thresholds) and IMA (three thresholds) [08:12], [08:42], [09:12].
- The speaker argues IMA helps with linemen because GPS-type measures are less reliable for high-intensity work in spaces under 20 meters [09:44].
- The joint model (total player load, player load low, impacts high) fit best; total player load and impacts high carried the highest added risk, and player load low was inversely related [14:20], [14:51], [15:22].
- Position group did not add explanatory value, possibly because of too few injuries per group [15:22], [15:53].
- Volume and intensity are risk factors to be combined with coaches' own judgment [15:53], [16:23].
- Injury is multifactorial; intrinsic and extrinsic factors and their change over a season would be needed for prediction [17:24], [17:54].

## Numbers and definitions

- Hundreds of millions: about 200 million dollars per year paid to players on injured reserve, in "some articles" [01:02].
- Knee injuries 3.1 per 1000 athlete exposures; hip and hamstring 2.2 per 1000 (ten years of NFL training camp data, cited work by "feely and colleagues", caption spelling) [02:03].
- Athlete exposure: one athlete in one game or training session [02:33].
- Season length: 16 NFL games, 9 to 13 in college [01:32].
- Sample: 101 football athletes, one full season preseason through regular season [11:14].
- Definition: non-contact injury that caused missed later sessions or games, coded by a medical professional [11:14], [11:45].
- Training load normalized per minute and standardized by position group [11:45], [12:15].
- Models: logistic regression, compared with Bayesian information criterion and out-of-sample likelihood, with leave-one-out-style cross validation [12:47], [13:18]. Caption reads "four logistic regression models" as "for"; model count is ambiguous (one per variable group plus a joint model).
- 29 non-contact injuries [13:18].
- Caption problems: the figure "200 million dollars" at [01:02] appears as captioned; "Bayesian information criterion" is clear; effect sizes (odds ratios) are not given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Catapult-type inertial sensors with player load, effort bands, impacts and IMA (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer) [08:12], [09:12].
- Censoring of athletes removed from a session by injury [12:15].
- Logistic regression and leave-one-out style validation on one season [12:47], [13:18].

## Limits and open questions

- One team, one season; 29 injuries is small and no position-group effect was found [13:18], [15:22].
- No game load, so no games injuries [16:53].
- Association only; the speaker says prediction would need intrinsic and extrinsic factors [17:24].
- Effect sizes and thresholds were not shown, and several injury types were pooled [16:23].
- Most injuries occurred in training camp, per Q&A [22:05].
- Underreporting of pain is a recognized limit [24:10].

## Q&A

- Is the problem data or random assignment, and could effort drive both load and injury? Random assignment would help if a coach agreed; effort perception data exist but were not in this paper [18:24], [19:27].
- A panelist said a full picture needs internal load, HRV, hydration, hip mobility asymmetry and pain, and RPE; the speaker said no research shows joint range or posture predicts injury, and measures would change during a season [19:59], [20:29].
- Did the 101 players include roster cuts and did the final 53 differ? Most injuries were in camp and effort looks similar across players, with starters managed more [21:35], [22:05].
- Medical-attention and contact injuries? They looked at time loss and non-time loss; underreporting is a big limit; contact injury and over-exertion link is plausible but hard to model [23:09], [24:10], [24:41].

Caption problems: model count at [12:47] ("for logistic regression models"), "Feely" and "Luke borne"/"Berry dress" co-author names may be mis-transcribed; Kendall's introduction title differs slightly from the video title.
